I think it goes up quite a lot, and that's one of the things I find most exciting right now.

Historically, there's been a gap between the data people could collect about themselves and what anyone could do with it. You could wear a fitness tracker, get bloodwork, maybe even sequence your genome, but turning that into an insight about you specifically required a clinician with time, context, and expertise, and most people don't get much of that. A doctor might spend fifteen minutes with you once a year looking at a handful of numbers. So a lot of personal health data just sat there. The bottleneck wasn't the data; it was the interpretation.

As models get more capable, that bottleneck starts to loosen. A model that can reason across your lab trends over five years, your sleep and heart rate data, your medications, your family history, and the latest literature can surface patterns that would be hard for any single person to catch. Something like "this marker has been drifting slowly in the wrong direction, and combined with these other signals it's worth a conversation with your doctor." The marginal value of each data point rises because there's finally something that can make use of it.

There's also a compounding effect over time. Longitudinal data is much more valuable than snapshots, because what's normal for you matters more than what's normal for the population. If you start collecting good data now, future models, which will likely be much better than today's, can look back over that history. In a sense you're banking context for a smarter interpreter you don't have access to yet.

That said, I'd add a few caveats. More data isn't automatically better. There's a real risk of overdiagnosis, anxiety, and chasing noise, and part of what good models need to do is tell you when something isn't worth worrying about. Data quality and provenance matter a lot too. And privacy becomes a bigger deal as the data becomes more valuable, so people should think about where it's stored and who controls it.

But the overall direction seems clear to me: as intelligence becomes cheap and abundant, personal context becomes the scarce input. The people and systems that have rich, well-organized health histories will get much more out of these models than those who don't.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly predicts that personal health data’s value will rise as models become more capable, explaining that stronger models can interpret and make use of more personal health information.

fable-5.1.text:
Karan Singhal: That's a great question, and I think the answer is that it makes personal health data much more valuable, not less. Historically, the bottleneck with self-collected health data hasn't really been collection, it's been interpretation. People have had step counts, sleep data, heart rate variability, maybe some lab results sitting in a portal, and the honest truth is that most of that data just sat there. Nobody had the time or the expertise to look across all of it and tell you something actionable. Even physicians, in a fifteen-minute visit, aren't going to pore over six months of your wearable data.

As models get more capable, that interpretive layer becomes something that can scale to everyone. A model can look at your sleep trends, your activity, your labs, your family history, the symptoms you mentioned offhand three weeks ago, and actually reason about how those fit together. And crucially, it can do that longitudinally, which is where a lot of the signal in health lives. A single reading is rarely that informative. The trajectory is.

So I'd frame it this way: the data you collect about yourself becomes the context that lets a very capable model actually personalize its reasoning to you rather than to the average patient in a trial. The more intelligent the model, the more it can extract from richer context. That shifts the incentive toward collecting more, and collecting more consistently.

There are a couple of caveats I'd add. One is that more intelligent models should also be better at telling you what's noise, so I don't think the answer is to obsessively measure everything. Part of the value is the model saying, this metric doesn't matter much for you, don't worry about it. The second is that this raises the stakes on privacy and on who controls that data, because if your personal health record is what makes an AI genuinely useful to you, then it's also quite sensitive. And the third is that we still need to be careful about how these systems handle uncertainty. A model confidently over-interpreting a wearable artifact is a real failure mode, and building systems that know when to escalate to a clinician rather than reassure or alarm is a big part of the work.

But directionally, I'm pretty convinced. Intelligence makes data more valuable, and personal health data is one of the clearest cases of that.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly says that as models become more capable, personal health data becomes more valuable, and concludes, “Intelligence makes data more valuable.”

astra-6.text:
I think it makes that data much more valuable. The usefulness of collecting health data depends on what you can do with it. If you have a continuous stream of measurements but no way to interpret them or make decisions based on them, the benefit is pretty limited.

As models get better, they could help put those measurements in context: what’s normal for you, what’s changed over time, and what might be worth discussing with a doctor. A single measurement can be hard to interpret; having your own baseline could make it much more informative.

So there’s potentially an option value to collecting data now. A future model might be able to extract something useful from that history that today’s models can’t. You can improve the analysis later, but you can’t go back and collect a measurement you never took. That doesn’t mean every measurement is worth collecting—there are costs, privacy concerns, and the risk of chasing noise—but I think better intelligence shifts that tradeoff toward having more useful longitudinal data.

r001.rationale: It says personal health data becomes much more valuable as models get better, explaining that improved intelligence can make collected measurements more useful.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it makes collecting that data much more valuable. Today, you might have years of sleep data or heart-rate data, and it’s hard to know what to do with it. But as models get smarter, they may be able to take that history, combine it with your medical records and what you’re experiencing, and help you understand patterns that would otherwise be difficult to see.

There’s an asymmetry here: you can wait for the models to improve, but you can’t go back and collect your baseline from five years ago. So I think there’s real option value in collecting good longitudinal data now, even if the immediate benefit is limited. That doesn’t mean measuring everything is useful, or that every fluctuation means something. But the ability to make sense of the data is improving, and that changes the value of having it.

r001.rationale: The response says personal health data becomes more valuable as models get smarter, explaining that improved models may reveal patterns in longitudinal data.
